## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Javanahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 476) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection told by the Buddha at Jetavana concerning the *Daḷhadhamma Suttanta* or "Parable of the Strong Men" [Bodhi 2003]. This introductory framework draws upon the theme of firm-bowed archers (*daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā*) [Bodhi 2003; Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a swift goose (*javanahaṁsa*) who performed a remarkable feat [Bodhi 2003; Fausböll 1887]. When invited by a human king to dwell with him, the king of the geese declined, reflecting that while the sounds of birds and jackals are easy to understand, the voice of human beings is far harder to decipher [Anandajoti 2010]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the human king is identified as Ānanda, the two goose brothers as Moggallāna and Sāriputta, the flock of geese as the Buddha's followers, and the swift goose as the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1887].
